analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.70 an hour, then $5.15 an hour.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage increase never left the Senate labor committee and never got a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in two steps: to $4.70 an hour starting in July 1995, and to $5.15 an hour starting in July 1996. The federal minimum was $4.25 at the time, so a full-time worker would have gained roughly $46 a week by 1996. The bill was introduced by Senator Tom Daschle with 21 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate labor committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the minimum wage — heavily concentrated in food service, retail, cleaning, and care work — would have seen their pay rise by law in two scheduled steps. Their employers would be required to pay the higher amounts, and workers who earn slightly above the new minimum would often see raises as pay scales adjust upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $4.25 to $4.70 an hour in the year beginning July 4, 1995, and to $5.15 an hour after July 3, 1996.
A full-time worker at the minimum wage would have earned about $46 more per week once the $5.15 rate took effect, roughly $2,400 a year before taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, farms, and small service businesses — bear the higher payroll costs. They can absorb those costs through higher prices, thinner margins, or reduced staffing and hours for entry-level jobs.

drawbacks.text: Employers of low-wage labor would face higher payroll costs, and small businesses operating on thin margins would feel them most; some would respond with higher prices, reduced hours, or fewer entry-level positions.

The bill contained no small-business offset or tip-related adjustment, so its costs fell directly on employers rather than being paired with tax relief, a point employers' groups pressed in the broader 1995–96 minimum wage debate.

Economists disagree about how much a minimum wage increase reduces employment among teenagers and entry-level workers; the bill's supporters argued the 1990–91 increase had caused little job loss, while opponents pointed to concentrated effects in the restaurant industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to see: several million low-wage workers would have taken home more pay, with the increase scheduled rather than left to annual political fights. The cost is real but narrower — higher labor bills for employers of minimum-wage labor, most visibly in food service and retail, with some risk of reduced entry-level hiring. The evidence from the 1990–91 federal increase, cited during this era's debates, suggested the employment cost was modest, though it fell on exactly the businesses with the least margin. The bill was plain-vanilla in design: a straight rate increase with no complicating provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, and it sat there without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the bill on February 14, 1995, joined on the day of introduction by ten Democratic senators including Edward Kennedy, Tom Harkin, and Paul Wellstone.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on February 14, 1995.
Twenty-one Democratic senators cosponsored the bill in addition to the sponsor.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee vote or floor consideration, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage labor — restaurant and retail chains and other low-wage employers — avoided the higher payroll costs the bill would have imposed, at least through January 1997. Workers at the minimum wage gained nothing from this bill, and the increase only arrived later through a different vehicle.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Original co-introducer of the bill on day one.

against.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never took it up; no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the record.

against.name: Sen. Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years the bill sat in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 supporters in the record were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Senate never took the bill up.

industries.note: The industry is the largest employer of minimum-wage workers and would have borne the largest payroll increase, which it typically offsets through menu prices and staffing. Workers at the minimum would have gained roughly $1,800–$2,400 a year.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retailers, hotels, cleaning firms, and small service businesses paying near the minimum would have seen payroll costs rise in two scheduled steps.
Roughly 10 million workers earned at or near the $4.25 minimum in the mid-1990s and would have received the legislated raises.
